    Prediction-Powered Sample Size Calculation

    Using n_required_ppi_pp() for Mean and Regression PPI/PPI++

    ppi-sample-size.Rmd

    Introduction

    Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) and PPI++ reduce labeled sample size needs by using a prediction model trained on large unlabeled datasets.

    This vignette demonstrates how to compute required required labeled sample size under:

    • Mean Estimation
    • OLS and GLM recression contrasts
    • Direct moments inputs or prediction metrics (confusion matrix, brier score, MSE, R2R^2, etc.)
    • Vanilla (PPI), Oracle, and user-specified λ\lambda (PPI++)

    All examples use the main function: n_required_ppi_pp() which solves for the smallest labeled sample size (n)(n) such that the asymptotic variance meets the target power level.

    Overview of the Sample Size Function

    The core function has the following interface:

    n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta, N,
  alpha = 0.05,
  power = 0.80,
  type = c("mean", "regression"),
  lambda_mode = c("vanilla", "oracle", "user"),
  lambda_user = NULL,
  # mean inputs
  sigma_y2, sigma_f2, cov_y_f,
  var_f, var_res,
  metrics, metric_type,
  # regression inputs
  c, H_L, H_U,
  Sigma_YY, Sigma_ff_l, Sigma_ff_u, Sigma_Yf,
  mode = c("error", "cap")
)

    Explanation:

    • delta: the effect size (c⊤β−c⊤β0)(c^\top \beta - c^\top\beta_0) for regression (OLS/GLM), or a shift in the mean.
    • N: size of the unlabeled dataset, typically very large.
    • alpha: Significance level (two-sided). Default value is 0.050.05.
    • power: Desired statistical power that you want to achieve. Default value is 0.800.80.
    • lambda_mode: determines whether λ\lambda is fixed at 1 (Vanilla PPI estimator), chosen by the user ("user"), or optimized ("oracle").
      • For mean mode, you may provide moments (sigma_y2, sigma_f2, cov_y_f) or prediction metrics (mse, var_f, accuracy, etc.).
        • For regression mode, you pass Hessians and covariance blocks computed by compute_ppi_blocks().

    Mean-Mode Sample Size — Direct Moments

    In the simplest case, you directly supply the population moments:

    • σy2=Var(Y)\sigma_y^2 = \mathrm{Var}(Y),
    • σf2=Var(f(X))\sigma_f^2 = \mathrm{Var}(f(X)),
    • Cov(Y,f)\mathrm{Cov}(Y,f)
    delta  <- 0.20
N      <- 3000
alpha  <- 0.05
power  <- 0.80

sigma_y2 <- 1.00
sigma_f2 <- 0.40
cov_y_f  <- 0.15

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta      = delta,
  N          = N,
  type       = "mean",
  lambda_mode = "vanilla",
  sigma_y2   = sigma_y2,
  sigma_f2   = sigma_f2,
  cov_y_f    = cov_y_f
)
#> [1] 222

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta      = delta,
  N          = N,
  type       = "mean",
  lambda_mode = "oracle",
  sigma_y2   = sigma_y2,
  sigma_f2   = sigma_f2,
  cov_y_f    = cov_y_f
)
#> [1] 186

    The stronger the correlation between outcome (YY) and the model prediction (f(X)f(X)), the more sample size reduction PPI++ yields relative to vanilla PPI.

    Mean-Mode Sample Size — Using Prediction Metrics

    Instead of providing moments, you can supply predictive performance metrics.

    metrics <- list(
  type    = "continuous",
  var_y   = 1.00,   # total outcome variance
  mse     = 0.20,   # very strong model (small residual error)
  var_f   = 0.80,   # predictions have high variance
  cov_y_f = 0.70,   # very high correlation model
  m_obs   = 500
)

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = 0.15,
  N           = 520,
  type        = "mean",
  lambda_mode = "vanilla",
  metrics     = metrics,
  metric_type = "continuous"
)
#> [1] 151

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = 0.15,
  N           = 520,
  type        = "mean",
  lambda_mode = "oracle",
  metrics     = metrics,
  metric_type = "continuous"
)
#> [1] 124

    m_obs is the number of labeled samples used to estimate the prediction metrics (MSE, variance, accuracy, etc.). Finite-sample corrections ensure the derived moments remain unbiased / feasible.

    Mean-Mode Sample Size — Using Confusion matrix

    You can also supply classifier performance through a confusion matrix:

    metrics <- list(
  type = "classification",
  # Confusion matrix (strong classifier)
  tp = 225,   # true positives
  fp =  25,   # false positives
  fn =  25,   # false negatives
  tn = 225,   # true negatives

  # Total observed labeled data used to compute the metrics
  m_obs = 500
)

# For reference:
# p_y = (tp + fn) / m_obs = (225 + 25)/500 = 0.50  (balanced)
# accuracy = (tp + tn)/500 = 450/500 = 0.90

# PPI sample-size calculation, λ=1
n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = 0.15,
  N           = 520,
  type        = "mean",
  lambda_mode = "vanilla",
  metrics     = metrics,
  metric_type = "classification"
)
#> [1] 43

# PPI++ oracle-λ
n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = 0.15,
  N           = 520,
  type        = "mean",
  lambda_mode = "oracle",
  metrics     = metrics,
  metric_type = "classification"
)
#> [1] 35

    For binary outcomes, the function internally computes:

    • prevalence (pyp_y)
    • prediction prevalence (pfp_f)
    • variance of residuals
    • covariance ( Cov(Y,f)\mathrm{Cov}(Y,f) )

    using identities derived from the confusion matrix.

    Regression-Mode Sample Size — OLS

    We now demonstrate the regression contrast mode.

    Generate Data:

    p    <- 4
n_l  <- 400
n_u  <- 3000
beta <- c(0.7, -0.5, 0.2, 1.0)

X_l <- matrix(rnorm(n_l*p), n_l, p)
X_u <- matrix(rnorm(n_u*p), n_u, p)

Y_l <- drop(X_l %*% beta + rnorm(n_l, sd = 0.7))
f_l <- drop(X_l %*% beta + rnorm(n_l, sd = 0.6))
f_u <- drop(X_u %*% beta + rnorm(n_u, sd = 0.6))

    Construct PPI++ blocks for sandwich variance estimators:

    blocks <- compute_ppi_blocks(
  model_type = "ols",
  X_l = X_l, Y_l = Y_l, f_l = f_l,
  X_u = X_u, f_u = f_u,
  beta = beta
)

    Solve sample size for contrast c⊤βc^\top \beta:

    c_vec <- c(0, 1, 0, 0)
delta <- as.numeric(t(c_vec) %*% beta)

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = delta,
  N           = n_u,
  power       = 0.90,
  type        = "regression",
  lambda_mode = "vanilla",
  c           = c_vec,
  H_L         = blocks$H_L,
  H_U         = blocks$H_U,
  Sigma_YY    = blocks$Sigma_YY,
  Sigma_ff_l  = blocks$Sigma_ff_l,
  Sigma_ff_u  = blocks$Sigma_ff_u,
  Sigma_Yf    = blocks$Sigma_Yf
)
#> [1] 35

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = delta,
  N           = n_u,
  power       = 0.90,
  type        = "regression",
  lambda_mode = "oracle",
  c           = c_vec,
  H_L         = blocks$H_L,
  H_U         = blocks$H_U,
  Sigma_YY    = blocks$Sigma_YY,
  Sigma_ff_l  = blocks$Sigma_ff_l,
  Sigma_ff_u  = blocks$Sigma_ff_u,
  Sigma_Yf    = blocks$Sigma_Yf
)
#> [1] 23

    Regression-Mode Sample Size — GLM: Logistic Regression

    (We follow similar steps as described in OLS case above)

    p    <- 3
n_l  <- 500
n_u  <- 2500
beta <- c(1.2, -0.6, 0.5)

X_l <- matrix(rnorm(n_l*p), n_l, p)
X_u <- matrix(rnorm(n_u*p), n_u, p)

eta_l <- drop(X_l %*% beta)
eta_u <- drop(X_u %*% beta)

prob_l <- plogis(eta_l)
prob_u <- plogis(eta_u)

Y_l <- rbinom(n_l, 1, prob_l)

f_l <- plogis(eta_l + rnorm(n_l, sd = 1.5))
f_u <- plogis(eta_u + rnorm(n_u, sd = 1.5))

    Construct PPI++ blocks for sandwich variance estimators similar to previous OLS case:

    blocks_glm <- compute_ppi_blocks(
  model_type = "glm",
  family     = "binomial",
  X_l = X_l, Y_l = Y_l, f_l = f_l,
  X_u = X_u, f_u = f_u,
  beta = beta
)

    Then solve for sample size:

    c_vec <- c(1, 0, 0)
delta <- as.numeric(t(c_vec) %*% beta)

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = delta,
  N           = n_u,
  type        = "regression",
  lambda_mode = "vanilla",
  c           = c_vec,
  H_L         = blocks_glm$H_L,
  H_U         = blocks_glm$H_U,
  Sigma_YY    = blocks_glm$Sigma_YY,
  Sigma_ff_l  = blocks_glm$Sigma_ff_l,
  Sigma_ff_u  = blocks_glm$Sigma_ff_u,
  Sigma_Yf    = blocks_glm$Sigma_Yf
)
#> [1] 60

n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta       = delta,
  N           = n_u,
  type        = "regression",
  lambda_mode = "oracle",
  c           = c_vec,
  H_L         = blocks_glm$H_L,
  H_U         = blocks_glm$H_U,
  Sigma_YY    = blocks_glm$Sigma_YY,
  Sigma_ff_l  = blocks_glm$Sigma_ff_l,
  Sigma_ff_u  = blocks_glm$Sigma_ff_u,
  Sigma_Yf    = blocks_glm$Sigma_Yf
)
#> [1] 41

    Handling infeasible cases

    If the required labeled (nn) exceeds the unlabeled (NN), the function throws an error by default (mode = "error"):

    out <- n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta = 0.03,
  N     = 1000,
  type  = "mean",
  sigma_y2 = 1,
  sigma_f2 = 0.2,
  cov_y_f  = 0.05,
  mode = "error"
)
#> Error: Infeasible: cannot find n satisfying required power.

    Switch to mode = "cap" to get an estimate of power at n=Nn = N:

    out <- n_required_ppi_pp(
  delta = 0.03,
  N     = 1000,
  type  = "mean",
  sigma_y2 = 1,
  sigma_f2 = 0.2,
  cov_y_f  = 0.05,
  mode = "cap"
)
#> Warning: Required n exceeds search range; capping to n = N = 1000. Achieved
#> power = 0.1297.

out
#> [1] 1000
#> attr(,"achieved_power")
#> [1] 0.1296782
attr(out, "achieved_power")
#> [1] 0.1296782

    Power Curve Visualization

    This chunk visualizes how required (nn) decreases as effect size grows, and how oracle λ\lambda for PPI++ estimator provides a clear reduction in sample size estimations over vanilla PPI:

    delta_grid <- seq(0.10, 0.40, length.out = 40)

## Shared parameters (mean-estimation case)
N       <- 3000
sy2     <- 1.0      # Var(Y)
sf2     <- 0.4      # Var(f)
cyf     <- 0.15     # Cov(Y, f)
lambda_user_value <- 0.70   # example user-specified λ

## Compute required n for each λ mode
results <- lapply(delta_grid, function(d) {
  data.frame(
    delta = d,
    vanilla = n_required_ppi_pp(
      delta       = d,
      N           = N,
      type        = "mean",
      lambda_mode = "vanilla",
      sigma_y2    = sy2,
      sigma_f2    = sf2,
      cov_y_f     = cyf
    ),
    oracle = n_required_ppi_pp(
      delta       = d,
      N           = N,
      type        = "mean",
      lambda_mode = "oracle",
      sigma_y2    = sy2,
      sigma_f2    = sf2,
      cov_y_f     = cyf
    ),
    user = n_required_ppi_pp(
      delta       = d,
      N           = N,
      type        = "mean",
      lambda_mode = "user",
      lambda_user = lambda_user_value,
      sigma_y2    = sy2,
      sigma_f2    = sf2,
      cov_y_f     = cyf
    )
  )
})

df <- bind_rows(results) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c("vanilla", "oracle", "user"),
               names_to = "mode",
               values_to = "n")

ggplot(df, aes(delta, n, color = mode)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      vanilla = "#1B9E77",
      oracle  = "#D95F02",
      user    = "#7570B3"
    ),
    labels = c(
      vanilla = "PPI (vanilla λ = 1)",
      oracle  = "PPI++ (oracle λ*)",
      user    = paste0("User λ = ", lambda_user_value)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Required Labeled Sample Size vs. Effect Size δ",
    subtitle = paste("N =", N, " unlabeled samples"),
    y = "Required labeled sample size n",
    x = "Effect size δ",
    color = "λ-mode"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

    Summary

    This vignette demonstrated:

    • How to compute PPI / PPI++ sample size for mean estimation and regression.
    • How to use direct moments or prediction metrics (continuous or classification).
    • How to incorporate OLS or GLM models into contrast-based inference.
    • When sample sizes become infeasible and how to handle caps.
    • How λ\lambda affects the required labeled sample size.

    PPI++ typically yields the smallest labeled sample size, especially when the prediction model is strong and the correlation ( Cov(Y,f(X))\mathrm{Cov}(Y,f(X)) ) is high.
